newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan dollar inches to eight-year low close.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan dollar inches to eight-year low close.

text.p: The Taiwan dollar closed at an eight-year low against its U.S. counterpart on Wednesday, reflecting the strength of the greenback in Tokyo and other overseas markets, dealers said.
The local dollar dipped as low as T$27.958 before ending at T$27.939 against Tuesday's T$27.925 close.
Wednesday's close surpassed a previous eight-year low T$27.926 marked last Wednesday. The local unit has not closed lower since finishing at T$28.03 on January 7, 1989.
Turnover through dealers was heavy at US$404 million.
"As the U.S. dollar turns stronger against the yen overseas, investors are testing the central bank's attitude -- whether it will allow the Taiwan dollar to depreciate," said one dealer.

"The answer seems to be 'yes', probably because when other currencies are falling sharply against the U.S. dollar, if the Taiwan dollar resists to fall, Taiwan makers' export competitiveness will weaken," the dealer said.
Dealers nevertheless reported seeing apparent central bank intervention in late trade, especially in the final minute, to slow the Taiwan dollar's depreciation.

Central bank governor Hsu Yuan-dong, speaking after the close of trading, gave his most explicit comment to date on the speculative pressures that have undermined several southeast Asian currencies in July -- saying Taiwan was not vulnerable.

"Our situation is different from that in southeast Asia," Hsu told reporters. "We have big foreign exchange reserves and a big trade surplus. Our economy is good. What happened in southeast Asia cannot happen here. We won't have any problem."
Taiwan's dollar was lower most of the day, struggling around recent intraday support of T$27.94, slipping to T$27.943 shortly before the close, and rebounded in the final minute.

"Since preventing the Taiwan dollar from depreciating would be unfair to exporters, the central bank likely will allow some depreciation, but I believe it would prefer a step-by-step, slow depreciation," said another dealer.
Dealers said Wednesday's session was marked by active outflows of foreign funds and non-delivery forward trading as well as brisk U.S. dollar demand from importers.
"Of course, there was some local and foreign speculation as many see a Taiwan dollar downtrend as inevitable," one dealer said.
